hero:
# Everything Football — Soccer Data Hub

**Multi-source football data platform with entity resolution, scheduled refresh, and static dashboards · Python · Supabase · GitHub Actions**

## Hero Overview

A production-shaped data platform for open football data: five independent sources fetched through one cached reader layer, resolved into a single player identity across providers, merged and cleaned into a Supabase Postgres warehouse that a scheduled pipeline keeps current twice a week. Coverage is 18 seasons of the Big-5 European leagues.

The front end is deliberately the opposite — three static HTML files with inline JavaScript, no build step and no dependencies, reading the warehouse directly over PostgREST with a read-only key. The Match Center reconstructs league position after every round from raw results and charts long-run club Elo against the league median; the Player dashboard renders per-season percentile cards with a bargain-versus-premium valuation verdict. The same fetch layer is also exposed as an MCP server so an agent can query the hub through the identical functions.

points.evidence: Five sources, one reader per file, every one routed through a single cached_fetch(source, dataset, params, produce, force) memoizer that writes a content-addressed parquet cache. Readers return a Manifest describing the cached artifact rather than a DataFrame, so callers decide when to materialise. Each source needed its own workaround: FBref requires patching soccerdata's league config before import and disambiguating a bare season string into a two-year code, football-data.co.uk is read with plain pandas because the library's own reader 503s on this host, and only FBref needs a browser at all — the rest are ordinary HTTP fetches.

FBref and Transfermarkt name the same footballer differently, so a cross-source identity has to be built rather than looked up. The xref pipeline runs a four-rung ladder — manual overrides, then a stored mapping file, then exact match, then fuzzy — with every rung guarded by birth year so a fuzzy hit on a common name cannot silently bind the wrong player, and token blocking to keep the fuzzy pass tractable. Downstream, players sharing both a name and a team are separated by a birth-year suffix.

Supabase Postgres is the single source of truth behind six table families — player season stats, transfers, the player xref, age curves, match results and club Elo — defined by 11 hand-applied SQL migrations that double as the schema record. Writes use a service-role key with 500-row chunked upserts and a float-to-Int64 repair pass; reads use an anon key under row-level security that permits nothing but SELECT, which is what makes it safe to ship that key to a static page. The read helper paginates at 1,000 rows so a large query cannot silently truncate.

A GitHub Actions workflow refreshes the warehouse twice weekly across five jobs. The league matrix that touches FBref runs strictly one at a time to avoid an IP block, while the match-results matrix — plain CSV, no scrape risk — runs fully parallel. The age-curve job depends on the season job and derives its output from the hub itself, because PostgREST aggregates are disabled. A separate workflow publishes the site to Pages only when site files change.

Three static HTML files with inline CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step, querying PostgREST directly. The Match Center takes a league and season, recomputes league position after every round client-side from raw match results, and plots the race as a bump chart where unselected clubs stay faint and clickable; a second panel charts full club Elo from 2008 against the league's median club. The Player dashboard scores each season as an output percentile against positional peers and issues a Bargain, Fair or Premium verdict from the gap between output and value percentile, degrading to no verdict where the underlying defensive and keeper metrics do not exist rather than inventing one.

The same fetch layer is wrapped as an MCP server so an agent can call it without a second implementation: three reader tools each returning a manifest dict, plus a hub_table tool for league, season and player-id filtered reads of the warehouse with an explicit row cap. No parallel code path — the agent surface and the Python package call the identical functions.

storyline:
## Context

Open football data is plentiful and mutually incompatible. FBref has the match statistics, Transfermarkt has the market values, football-data.co.uk has the results, ClubElo has the strength ratings, and none of them agree on what a given player or club is called. Any question that spans two of them — is this player producing more than he costs, has this club actually been getting stronger — is really an entity-resolution problem wearing an analytics costume. The goal was a hub where that resolution happens once, on a schedule, so the dashboards on top can be simple.

## Workflow

Readers fetch each source into a content-addressed parquet cache → the xref pipeline resolves player identity across providers → the player_season pipeline merges statistics with values and cleans the result → chunked upserts land it in Supabase → a twice-weekly cron re-runs the whole path → static dashboards and an MCP server read the warehouse through the same row-level-security policy.

## Technical Implementation

- Reader layer: one file per source, each returning a Manifest rather than a DataFrame, all routed through a single cached_fetch memoizer so caching, forcing and cache-key logic exist in exactly one place.
- Source-specific workarounds: patching soccerdata's league config before import, mapping a bare season string to a two-year code, and reading football-data.co.uk with plain pandas because the library reader fails on this host. Only FBref needs a browser; everything else is plain HTTP.
- Entity resolution: a four-rung ladder — overrides, mapping file, exact, fuzzy — every rung guarded by birth year, with token blocking to keep the fuzzy pass fast.
- Cleaning rules that live in code and tests rather than prose: per-90 rates nulled below 450 minutes, age derived from birth year, a primary position picked per season, and a staleness flag on market values.
- Warehouse: 11 hand-applied migrations across six table families; service-role writes in 500-row chunks with a float-to-Int64 repair; anon reads under RLS that permits only SELECT, which is what makes shipping the key to a static page safe.
- Automation: five cron jobs twice weekly, with the FBref-touching matrix serialised to avoid an IP block and the CSV-based matrix left fully parallel.
- Front end: three static files, no build step, no dependencies. The Match Center recomputes league position round by round from raw results client-side; the Player dashboard scores seasons as percentiles against positional peers and refuses to issue a verdict where the underlying metrics do not exist.
- Testing: 64 tests across 17 files, entirely monkeypatched, so the suite covers the merge and cleaning rules without ever touching the network.

## Outcomes

A self-refreshing warehouse covering 18 seasons of the Big-5 leagues — 32,545 match records and roughly 191,000 club Elo rows — with one resolved player identity spanning five providers, and dashboards that read it directly with no server of their own. The known seams are recorded rather than hidden: club names still differ across sources behind an interim alias map, and upserts cannot delete, so a changed key leaves orphans that need a manual sweep.
